citation: "Tremont House." Chicagology. Compiling city-directory entries 1846-1870, an uncredited building summary, Chicago Illustrated (January 1866) by James W. Sheahan, and a reader's letter headed "THE FOUR TREMONTS", Chicago Tribune, 2 February 1874.
locator: The uncredited "Building Summary" paragraph beginning "The first Tremont House, a three-story wooden building"; the Chicago Illustrated, January 1866 section; and the Chicago Tribune, 2 February 1874 letter "THE FOUR TREMONTS" with its sub-heads "The Muddy Days" and "The First Fire".
note:
THE SOURCE OF "A MERE SHELL", AND IT IS AN 1874 LETTER TO A NEWSPAPER. Verbatim, under the Tribune date of 2 February 1874: "In 1833 there was built upon the northwest corner of Lake and Dearborn streets an unpretending frame structure known as the Tremont House, and the following year Ira Couch became its proprietor. He found the house a mere shell, without any sidewalk around it, and poorly furnished, as none of the rooms were entirely carpeted, little pieces in front of the bed being considered sufficient for anyone; and very many of the beds were minus one pleasant luxury, a pillow." And under "The Muddy Days": "Around this corner, in early spring-time, it was impossible to drive the stage, and the passengers had to walk some two blocks; on account if the marshy state of the ground, the horses could not navigate" (the "if" for "of" is the page's). And under "The First Fire": "In the fall of 1839, the Tremont House was first consumed by fire."

THE STOREY COUNT IS WEAKER THAN THE DOSSIER MAKES IT LOOK. docs/research/04-structures-south.md line 155 records the height as contested and says "chicagology and Wikipedia say three-story wooden", and adopts three. On this page the ONLY sentence giving a storey count is the uncredited editorial summary: "The first Tremont House, a three-story wooden building at the northwest corner of Lake and Dearborn streets, was built in 1833." Neither period text on the page counts storeys. The 1874 letter says "an unpretending frame structure". Chicago Illustrated (January 1866) says "The first house making any pretensions to the character of a hotel was a wooden structure, called the 'Tremont House,' on the north-west corner of Lake and Dearborn streets, owned and kept by the brothers Couch." So chicagology's three storeys is one modern uncredited sentence, not a witness, and it should not be weighed as though it were independent of Wikipedia. What the page's period texts DO agree on, twice and separately, is the north-west corner and frame construction.

DO NOT READ THE PAGE HEADER. Its metadata block says "Address: SE corner of Lake and Dearborn Streets" and "Architect: John M. Van Osdel". Both belong to the later Tremonts - Van Osdel's is the 1850 brick house - and the header flatly contradicts every body text on the same page about the first building. The header also gives "Tremont I (1833-1839), Tremont II (1839-1849)" while the 1874 letter in the body has Couch erecting Tremont No. 2 "in 1841". Take the corner and the dates from the body, not the header.
